local.title: The Brevard County jail
local.lead: Melbourne Beach has its own police department but no jail. People arrested anywhere in Brevard County are taken to the county’s Jail Complex in Cocoa, which the county owns and the Sheriff runs. Town residents help pay for it through the county property tax.

facts.v: 1,849 rated beds — a main jail that opened in 1986 with 386 beds, plus four tent housing structures, an annex, and a mental health and medical unit. It “routinely houses over 1,600 inmates daily.”

src.label: Brevard County Sheriff’s Office — Jail Complex

facts.v: In February 2023 the jail averaged 1,431 people a day. 1,242 of them — 86.8% — had not been convicted: 1,073 awaiting trial on felonies and 169 on misdemeanors. That is the most recent count found (Docket #10).

src.label: Florida Dept. of Corrections — County Detention Facilities, Feb. 2023

facts.v: The Sheriff asked for $61,480,102 to run the jail in FY2025-26, up from $56,846,614 — $46.8 million of it for staff. Jail food and medical care alone is $13,402,347. That is roughly $91 per bed per day. The adopted FY2026-27 figure isn’t found yet (Docket #10).

A year ago the Sheriff counted 577 open repair and replacement work orders at the jail. At the county’s September 2026 budget hearing he described a 40-year-old jail with over 690 open work orders and asked for at least $3.5 million a year for repairs.

Already offered, by request and with classification approval: GED prep and testing; barber licensing, ServSafe manager certification, OSHA 30, traffic flagger, sewing, garment printing, floor care, canine training (Paws & Stripes); the Sheriff’s Farm; AA, NA, parenting, finance, and a veterans program (SAVE). The Sheriff says the trade programs give “a practical skill, which will lead to certification.”

The Sheriff’s Farm started in the 1980s as an alternative to a prison sentence. In 2017 it farmed 13 acres, with one potato crop expected to yield 35,000–40,000 pounds for the jail kitchen. Jail crews also keep up the lawns of 28 county properties (362 acres), which the Sheriff values at $265,000 a year.
The jail’s budget lists $48,000 a year from Eastern Florida State College as a “Veterinary Technician” reimbursement. What that program teaches, and to whom, isn’t described (Docket #11).
The local circuit runs a voluntary drug court: 12 to 18 months of treatment, and the felony charge is dismissed on completion. It also runs a veterans treatment court.

This year’s town budget pays for a chief, a deputy chief, two sergeants, two corporals and six officers — $1,677,353, the town’s largest department. One officer is the school resource officer, paid back by the School Board.

proposals.title: Grow the farm into a college credential
proposals.summary: The Sheriff’s Farm already feeds the jail, and the jail already teaches trades that end in a certificate. Join the two with the county’s own college: an Eastern Florida State College certificate in horticulture, food safety, or equipment operation, earned on the farm and in the kitchen and finished after release.
proposals.why_here: The jail costs about $61 million a year, and most people inside haven’t been convicted and won’t stay long — so a credential has to be short and portable. The college already sends the jail money for one program.
proposals.first_step: Ask the Sheriff and Eastern Florida State College to pilot one short farm-and-kitchen certificate, tracking who finishes, who gets hired, and who comes back.

ask.label: Weigh in on the open question

proposals.title: An offered work crew that builds homes
proposals.summary: Every morning the crew is offered: wake up, eat, and go build — or stay in the cell. Crew members earn pay and real credentials working alongside a licensed builder on homes for local families, through a partner like Habitat for Humanity or a community land trust. Some will stick with it after release; either way, the community gets stronger.
math: about 640 people — far more than one builder can lead, so crews would be small and rotating
Labor per modest 1,200 sq ft house (ordinary construction)
about 1,000 on-site hours (BLS: 82 hours per 100 sq ft)
set by money and crew leaders, not by labor
limits: Labor isn’t the limit — money is. At the national average of about $162 a square foot, a 1,200 sq ft house costs roughly $195,000 to build, before land. On a barrier island, land is the biggest cost of all.
Most people are held for weeks, so the crew is always partly new; it needs paid, trained crew leads — often people who stayed on after release.
Houses given to families work best through a nonprofit or land trust; what a county may give away is a question for a lawyer.

proposals.title: A door you can walk in
proposals.summary: Some people know they need structure before a crime ever happens. Offer a voluntary live-in program — housing, work, training, recovery — that a person can choose to enter and is free to leave. Choosing structure without a record is honor preserved.
limits: Nobody can be locked up without a crime or a court order, so it must stay a door that opens both ways.
“Voluntary” can be bent by desperation or a judge’s pressure; the design must guard against both.
Residents’ work must be paid and for their own growth — never unpaid labor for a company.
